pages.html:
A conversation between Chief Engineer at The State Dave Neale and Anna Best...

Dave: some weeks later english heritage came in, now you see if I might say this they all wear jesus sandals and all seem to have beards - yes they do

Anna: really

Dave: yes they do, I dont know why it is - and they're all vegetarian and I mean

Anna: well I'm vegetarian

Dave: yes and as I say there's nothing wrong in any of that but for some reason that seems to be their code of dress, anyway, two of them came down, very nice people, I've met them before...

Anna: how did they first get involved here - English heritage

Dave: well they were the people who got the building listed. We got them - I got them involved

Anna: did you? did you think this building has to be listed and...?

Dave: oh yeah twenty years ago it was under serious threat it really was the company wanted to pull it down and unfortunately you see theyd started to take the ruthless pills by then - they take even more now
pages.caption: Dave and Anna

pages.html:
Anna: started to take what?

Dave: the ruthless pills

Anna: ruthless pills?

Dave: yeah the pills to make them ruthless every day

Anna: who?

Dave: the higher executives and people higher up......

Anna: what a lot of people from Rank?

Dave: ......so naturally you see they have to make hard headed business decisions which means automatically places like this must be knocked down and you must build a new one which is gonna make you more money which is of course absolute nonsense

Anna: it's a very short sighted ruthless pill

Dave: yes yes yes its not an intelligence pill its just a ruthless pill. anyway myself and a few other interested people we thought wed take them to court - they'd taken the organ console away

Anna: what's the console?
pages.caption: Dave and Anna

pages.html:
Dave: just the bit you see up there I'll show you that in a moment - and they left all the pipe work up there which meant it couldnt be played so we took them to court we got the organ back and we saved the building. anyway this particular architect of course unbelievably had painted the building without getting permission to change the colour scheme

Anna: oh wow

Dave: now that which you see up there is virtually identical to the original colour scheme

Anna: oh is it? sort of brown and turquoise colours? right so that's more original than the new one

Dave: yes that's virtually identical to how I remember it when I first came here in 51 and looking at the original drawings and various pieces of information it seems that that was what the colour scheme basically was. But then you see when it was built as a cinema we didnt need the sort of bright lights that people need now for people to play bingo with right, we need obviously totally different lighting - our corporate image is different now and people who play bingo expect to see garishly coloured buildings to be perfectly honest

Anna: what's that all about then? Why does bingo have to have bingo colours?

Dave: well they're a different type of person to those that would go to cinemas I mean they could be identical people but when they go to cinemas they expect different things to when they go to a bingo club
pages.caption: Dave and Anna

pages.html:
Anna: it's a different mood or something isnt it - a different atmosphere

Dave: I presume so yeah anyway this gentleman came down from english heritage and he said I'm sorry but we must insist that the building is repainted......

Anna: he said that to the architect?

Dave: .....and the architect flew off the handle because he didn't believe that english heritage had got any authority whatsoever and unfortunately for him they have - they're the ultimate authority as far as listed buildings go

Anna: what colours had he painted it though?

Dave: these colours that you see now

Anna: the more pink and purple - is it purple? is it mauve?

Dave: well pink and sort of purpley mauve the like of which if it were a cinema would not be appropriate colours at all

Anna: they're too bright aren't they

Dave: yes but for the purposes for which we use it now it's you know more in keeping with shall we say the lower ...... so but you see that the main thing is that he didnt apply for permission to change the colour scheme
pages.caption: Dave and Anna

pages.html:
Anna: right - which is pretty foolish for an architect

Dave: well that's why you employ an architect you expect him to deal with all those sorts of things

Anna: you expect him to know all the rule and regulations

Dave: exactly I mean although as he pointed out I wasnt an architect I did know those rules and regulations you know on a listed building anything above a grade three you have to apply for permission to do almost anything

Anna: any changes, yeah sure

Dave: any alterations at all

Anna: so is this grade one

Dave: grade two but its soon to be grade one

Anna: is it? right, that's really good, yeah

Dave: yeah we've been trying now for ages to ....... because about 4 years ago we started the process - 4 or 5 years ago it came under threat again.

Anna: oh really? god from the same ruthless people
pages.caption: Dave and Anna

pages.html:
Dave: yes well you see how can I explain it - our corporate image now - they've got this obsession about what is known as a flat floor building

Anna: what does that mean?

Dave: well they believe the modern purpose built bingo halls that are on one level, air conditioned and extremely bang up to date and modern are the only sort of buildings that would succeed. now obviously thats a total nonsense because they spent 11 million pounds building one in Beckton which stayed open for less than 2 years - it's now shut

Anna: really?

Dave: yes but there are some that work but they don't work necessarily because they're flat floor and modern. we've got one in southend very very busy but there isnt another bingo club within thirty miles of if

Anna: so it's about other factors

Dave: yes but there's this belief this absolute belief that they are the only buildings that work and that these sort of places do not work anymore

Anna: does this work commercially?

Dave: it does work commercially yes but we dont make as much money and we dont do as much business as we used to.
pages.caption: Dave and Anna

pages.html:
Dave: .......now the reason why they justify their argument - up the road in cricklewood youve got a brand new flat floor building or rather it isnt a flat floor building there is actually a gallery inside it there is an upper level but it is in a brand new building and it does do tremendous business but you see it doesnt do tremendous business because of the type of building that it is

Anna: no it must be about demographics or what?

Dave: well it's where it is - the money reason why it does so well is very simple. one the owner of it is a guy called Jimmy Thomas who is an entrepreneurial character he's the arthur daily of the bingo world for want of a better description. I've known him many years

Anna: there's an Arthur Daly of every world isn't there

Dave: yes there is. the guy could make money he'd sell sand to the arabs he would

Anna: he's a friend of yours? you know him?

Dave: well he's an acquaintance he's not a friend but he's an acquaintance and he's built that building there because he wanted to shut this one down because he was in......

Anna: wow and then he'd take over - he'd have a bigger catchment
pages.caption: Dave and Anna

pages.html:
Dave: well he'd nab our business of which he's taken half

Anna: has he? why did he want to shut this down?

Dave: ....he had a contractual argument with Rank. he used to own a company called thomas automatics that made all these fruit machines

Anna: that was his company?

Dave: his company we bought it

Anna: oh

Dave: and there was some mysterious problem between the two companies and this at the time he thought was the biggest and best club that we got. well it was arguable business wise - certainly sidewise yes it's the biggest unit we operate - business wise it probably wasnt but anyway he wanted to shut it down to prove that he was a better business man than all the people at Rank which he obviously is because he does more business than us I dont think any body argues with that situation but any way it hasnt happened. hes shut three other clubs and prevented a fourth from being built - three other bingo clubs in this area have closed since he opened up weve survived and were now doing reasonably well. there is no chance he would ever shut this place down because it had to stay open the company has got to maintain a business here because they cannot shut it - it sends the wrong message does it not !
pages.caption: Dave and Anna

pages.html:
Anna: if they shut

Dave: if they shut it means that anybody could then open up a bingo club near by and we would then shut our one down

Anna: yeah presumably this is a bit of a flag ship isn't it ? or not?

Dave: it is when it suit's them

Anna: yeah right

Dave: now this is a very cynical view and unfortunately over the last 15 years ive become somewhat cynical with the company. they believe you see that the future of bingo is these flat floor buildings

Anna: and that just means no upper circle, purpose built and no steps?

Dave: yes on one level alone and we've got several that have been perfectly successful but it is not entirely due to the fact that they're single level buildings there are other things to consider for example he came into here one day and he said to me youve been here a long time he said who is the most difficult customer youve got and I pointed out the one who swears at us the most and carries on the most and pointed her out and he went and sat and spoke to her for twenty minutes and every other word was 'f' and you know and so on
pages.caption: Dave and Anna

pages.html:
Anna: what from her - right

Dave: yes but he sat and listened right and he came away with far more information than he could ever get from anyone else. admittedly some of her complaints were unrealistic but he still listened to what she had to say

Anna: and he was like the top 'mr big'

Dave: yeah 'mr big, you see now of course you would not get them here... somebody would do a report which would appear on the front of mr big's computer screen but it would not be based on talking to anybody personally here

Anna: that's interesting what would they do questionnaires?

Dave: yeah it would be based on market research

Anna: how's that done by Rank?

Dave: well you tell me

Anna: do they put out questionnaires and stuff Rank?

Dave: no

Anna: or do they just make it up?
pages.caption: Dave and Anna

pages.html:
Dave: they make it all up how else could they do it? I have never seen a market research company come in here and speak to the members how else are they gonna find out?

Anna: well absolutely - I completely agree

Dave: what way can they find out? what was the fellow that used to be that mad, john (a member of staff who's just joined the conversation), he had the double barrelled name?

Anna: oh god I cant think -

Dave: he was a bit of an aristocrat wasnt he - awfully posh

Anna: was it quite a while ago?

Dave: yeah it was quite a few years ago now ill think of his name and anyway - wait I can give you another for-instance - do you remember the market research company? we had to carry their video camera up onto the roof do you remember that?

Anna: yeah yeah yeah what was that from?

Dave: we had to carry this video camera and tripod up onto the main roof and they were filming the area obviously it's quite good view from up there it's a very high building
pages.caption: Dave and Anna

pages.html:
Anna: oh wow yeah

Dave: I could not resist asking them why

Anna: why are you filming kilburn!

Dave: we want to make a video of the area for the club and were gonna send it to all the members that havent been for a while so I said all right fine why aren't you taking one of the inside? they could not give me a satisfactory explanation as to why they were up on the roof. and dont you remember trevor was a bit of a....?

Anna: oh trevor!

Anna: who's trevor? a guy who worked here?

Dave: yeah and he was a bit of a womaniser shall we say and this young lady had a very short skirt on and trevor was waiting with anticipation as to whether she was gonna go up the stairs case or not but it was quite humorous the situation and she suddenly realised and she didnt go up there she sent the bloke up there and trever was most disappointed and it was all very funny but having said that we laughed more at the absurdity of it all you know it really was quite absurd

Anna: so that was part of market research
pages.caption: Dave and Anna

pages.html:
Dave: yeah what was the name? their companys called marketing solutions I think and of course obviously somebody higher up saw it and thought what a load of old rubbish you know and they were half a billion pounds in debt

Anna: mecca were?

Dave: yeah 536 million pounds in debt

Anna: were mecca always bingo?

Dave: this was the bingo side of it we bought there is mecca bookmakers which split from that company many many years ago right the point im trying to make is we got most of their executives and senior staff ours went

Anna: how weird if they've run a company.....

Dave: yeah well this is the peculiar thing we had adopted the methods of a company that were half a billion pounds in debt

Anna: how strange

Dave: and our profit forecasts and our figures are going the same way

Anna: wow
pages.caption: Dave and Anna

pages.html:
Dave: am I being too simplistic by saying im not surprised we were always the most successful people in this business - in the leisure industry full stop

Anna: Rank

Dave: yes we were better at it than anybody else but no longer - no longer and when you hear of someone coming out with crazy decisions like that making every club the same price and same opening times....

Anna: yeah that is crazy

Dave: ....you have to say to yourself right it might be cheaper to run head office that way but it's not gonna make us any money - at the end of the day it's bums on seats that counts

Anna: yeah yeah that is ridiculous

Dave: .....they built it because you know when it was built 61 years ago kilburn was a depressed area because most of the irish people that had been born into the area for building the railways - there was no major railway building like that to do it had all been done - so it was much as you see it now there was lots of unemployed people and it wasnt a particularly wealthy area and yet just a few hundred yards down the road can find a few one million pound houses

Anna: is that hampstead?
pages.caption: Dave and Anna

pages.html:
Dave: no wilsden just down the road here I could take you within a ten minute walking distance and show a house that was sold recently for 5 million pounds v: is that maida vale?

Dave: no that's way up there no I'm saying just down here just off wilsden lane anyway the only reason they built it here was because it was the only plot of land that they could find that was big enough which is an imaginably simple answer really

Anna: that's very pragmatic, I like that

Dave: well it is yes I mean it was the nearest large plot of land to the centre of london and they didnt want to go right in the centre of london because they didnt want to be too near to the leicester square theatres which were the most important ones even in those days. this was the first release house when it was built which the odeon leicester square wasnt.......

Anna: oh really

Dave: .....it was the trocadero that was used for things like that although royalty did come here on a couple of occasions anyway to give you some idea of the out lay your average provincial cinema would be built for between 40,000 and 60,000 in those days this cost 358,000 to build and unfortunately as he will admit readily if he was still here they ran out of money
pages.caption: Dave and Anna

pages.html:
Anna: phil

Dave: phil hyams had run out of money and the project was taken over by the gaumont british picture corporation

Anna: did they make all the gaumont's cinemas

Dave: they owned all the gaumonts and nobody knew at the time of course that the gaumont had a parent company called the cinema managements association which was owned by old j arthur himself - nobody knew that

Anna: whos j arthur?

Dave: j arthur Rank

Anna: oh god no one knew it - would that make a difference?

Dave: Yes well, it would have done because obviously he was in direct competition with the americans for making films and shortly before the war he built pinewood studios which was bigger and still is than anything they've got out there. what he wasn't going to be held to was that he was determined that he wasnt going to be dictated to by the hollywood film moguls so he made his own films at his own film studios he had four or five

Anna: that was sixty one years ago
pages.caption: Dave and Anna

pages.html:
Dave: no well the project was started in 34 it didnt open until december 20th 37 he took - well gaumont british took the project over approximately half way through. it was originally going to be called the troxy - sorry the roxy (troxy hed already got a troxy) he was going to call it the roxy the reason they were gonna call it the roxy and the reason according to phil hyams they wanted to call it the roxy was that the largest cinema at that time in the world was the roxy new york built by a fella called ratfouler - they wanted to built a place bigger than the americas

Anna: so it's a bit like the space thing like who can build the biggest rocket

Dave: well it was a race yes. mgm had built the empire leicester square - that was their main place, odeon cinemas had not come into existence as a separate company in those days not by then most of the Odeon cinemas in those days were acquisitions there wasnt an odeon cinema built until 38 not a purpose built one there were many open before that but theyd been changed from something else right the very first odeon was in perry bar in birmingham which was 1931

Anna: the first one that was built or just opened?

Dave: no the first opened as an odeon

Anna: so what sort of buildings did cinemas use?

Dave: well they were cinemas but they were other peoples and they were either leased or....
pages.caption: Dave and Anna

pages.html:
Anna: oh right ok got you yeah

Dave: .....not a lot of people know this but most of the odeon cinemas that were opened before the war were owned by railway companies yes because they were built on their land and they saw it as a means of generating capital and some of our odeon cinemas still are owned by railway companies not the building the land. I cant remember them all I mean the nearest I know of to here is be barking odeon which used to be owned by b r who the hell owns it now ive no idea

Anna: yeah right probably about three private railway companies

Dave: probably someone owns the lights somebody owns the bricks and mortar and so on but anyway to get back to this one it was a major cinema project nobody but no one had ever spent that amount of money building a cinema before not even the americans had spent that much money - it's not often weve got something thats bigger and grander than them but now you see it was an arguable point when it opened up it was called the gaumont steak - it wasnt called the roxy they didnt want that name it was called the gaumont state - the architect of the building george coles had been to new york and hed seen the empire state building and he thought - and hed put it in his memoirs - what a wonderful idea to build a miniature empire state building and use it as a front piece for a cinema and he put the project to hyams brothers and he thought yes lets do it

Anna: lovely! that's why it's called the state
pages.caption: Dave and Anna

pages.html:
Dave: yes thats why it's called the gaumont state - gaumont after the gaumont picture corporation, state after the empire state building. now we get back to this subject of size again. the roxy new york could seat 6254 people and it had 2 balconies weve only got one but that had two balconies. this building could seat 4004 but could also stand 4000 so you hold 8004 people

Anna: stand - where did they stand up or down?

Dave: well all sorts of places anyway the actual floor area was greater than that of the roxy new york to be honest I never saw the place but ive seen the drawings and ive seen lots of pictures. it was pulled down in 1960 BREAK

Dave: you'd have gone up the circle stairs into the circle lounge where you would have had a choice you'dve either gone into the cinema to watch the film or you'dve gone into the restaurant which became the little cinema and we used to do five programmes a day in those days so it was continuous 12 till 12 because you paid one and six or two shillings for the privilege of coming up here. I dont suppose you know what that means do you?

Anna: no I don't know

Dave: well it was 7.5p or 10p in new money to come up here. downstairs was ninepence which translates - the nearest I can think - to about 3.5p
pages.caption: Dave and Anna

pages.html:
Anna: so it was more than double - this room is totally amazing

Dave: this was the circle lounge - there was a cloak room there, there was a ladies cosmetic room in there, there was telephone boxes over there, there was couches to lounge in to wait in if you wanted to

Anna: and were people drinking and smoking (Dave: yeah) and being served

Dave: yeah) and all that stuff (Dave: yeah) wow

Dave: Over there in the corner was the bar there were sets of doors there that went straight into the restaurant - which became the little cinema

Anna: so what's there now?

Dave: it's still the little cinema - it's there but it's shut obviously

Anna: can we have a look

Dave: it's a bit difficult today but another day p'raps when we've got more time obviously

Anna: ok fine sure

Dave: but there was every conceivable luxury - there was iced water fountains downstairs which was unheard of cinemas, there was ladies awaiting your pleasure in the cosmetic room
pages.caption: Dave and Anna

pages.html:
Anna: to help you powder your nose?

Dave: whatever do whatever you know. we had a nurse on duty all the time in case any one was unwell which didnt happen any where else you know that didnt stop until the late sixties when we got rid of the nurse

Anna: this is kind of like an ocean liner or something isn't it

Dave: in a way I suppose yes the thing that did annoy me though we had a huge semi-circular leather settee there and our managing director pinched it - if ever Id come close to committing murder it was then - so you'd decided to come in and watch the film you'd come up either of these two entrances

Anna: does anyone come up here now dave (Dave: no) not at all?

Dave: no only me, it's unused - be careful how you go round here cos obviously it's dusty round here. although the company painted all of this we operate as a flat floor none of this up here is ever used we operate as a flat floor (v: whys that?) well it's a long story your colleague will tell you

Anna: ill tell you about flat floors - Rank and their flat floor obsession

Dave: so anyway obviously this level has been raised to enable us to build these tables cos when we first did the conversion sixteen years ago we did use this part
pages.caption: Dave and Anna

pages.html:
Anna: for bingo?

Dave: yes for bingo and it was actually quite popular a lot of people liked it even those tip up seats even those you'd be surprised they liked them

Anna: well it's nice to be up here

Dave: but what you get - see bingo people are a funny bunch - you got seats there for 4 people two either side you'd never ever get 4 people sat there unless they came as a group you'll get two people sat there and heaven help any body tried to sit next to them it's just they're a strange......

Anna: it's a bit like that down there isn't it?

Dave: it is yes ..... they're a strange bunch in the sense that they've got their own seats I remember a classic case. the first big bingo club that we did was wood green it was the old gaumont palace wood green

Anna: what do you mean the first one you did - changed from a...?

Dave: the first one where we spent serious money

Anna: to turn it from cinema to bingo?
pages.caption: Dave and Anna

pages.html:
Dave: yes we spent half a million pounds in 83 neither us nor our competitors had spent that kind of money before. they were converted for sort of 50,000 at the most. wed spent half a million doing it all up making it look very nice any way it opened on a Thursday evening but the Saturday previously wed had a sort of an open morning. people were allowed to come in and see what it looked like and wed give them a free cup of tea and show them how wonderful it was you know a bit of pre publicity. that thursday night when I opened up there was a fight amongst these different groups two groups of people and I managed to separate them and I said to them what the hell are you fighting for he sat in my seat said this woman and I said but we only opened an hour ago how can that be your seat? - I was hear last saturday

Anna: wow

Dave: 'oh my god I just cant believe you people weve got near 2000 seats in that place' - it's the same here weve got two and half thousand seats and yet they'll argue over one. wander down here you'll get some idea of the grandeur of the place.

Anna: do you still use that?

Dave: the wurlitzer is used yes - sadly I was gonna give you a quick demo but

Anna: oh can you play it?
pages.caption: Dave and Anna

pages.html:
Dave: yes I can

Anna: oooh!

Dave: but sadly at the moment the blower motor is out of action im awaiting a phone call from the engineering place that have new shaft and barings made for the blower motor

Anna: do you still have - is it every other Sunday morning?

Dave: no no it wouldnt be possible to do that. we do about six concerts a year

Anna: when's the next one?

Dave: hopefully 7th feb and there's an extra one if you do get chance to come to one concert this year come on march 28th

Anna: will do definitely yeah

Dave: because for definite it will be back in action by then

Anna: march 28th - is something else happening? isn't there a national competition for what we saw on the stage last time?

Dave: oh that - I dont know - that is in march sometime yeah but this'll be on the Sunday morning
pages.caption: Dave and Anna

pages.html:
Anna: yeah I'd really really like to know really like to know about that

Dave: well try and keep a note of that date because there's somebody very special going to be playing

Anna: 7th feb 28th march. it's not this woman ena...ena berger

Dave: ena barger no not her no not her shes actually now retired she is actually packed up which is sad but she is ninetyseven after all wonderful lady wonderful lady.....

Anna: yeah you told us about her before and she sounded really interesting

Dave: .....one of the great eccentrics and mean that sincerely one of the great eccentrics she sort of I don't know queen victoria miss marple and maggie thatcher all rolled into one I suppose she's just a wonderful character she really is albeit that my ribs get sore every time she comes in - pokes me with that damn stick of hers

Anna: so who's playing on 28th?

Dave: it's a fella called john mann and he is a very special player he's a good friend of mine I've known him many years and he is a very special player you'll be surprised what he can do with that thing

Anna: mmmm I'd love to yeah
pages.caption: Dave and Anna

pages.html:
Dave: yes unfortunately hence the reason for the little hammond down there because we were gonna sing christmas carols just before christmas to the members and the organ went wrong which is very annoying and it'll cost a couple of grand

Anna: to fix it ?

Dave: well it will do yes to get it fixed but then having said that I mean

Anna: do you get grants for things like that - do Rank pay ?

Dave: no not a penny

Anna: who pays?

Dave: myself - other members of the organ society

Anna: oh really? really? Rank dont pay to fix it?

Dave: not a penny, no not a penny piece

Anna: god!

Dave: but then you see this is the annoying factor about it - you remember you said to me is this their flag ship place? if ever they want to impress anybody they bring them here
pages.caption: Dave and Anna

pages.html:
Anna: well course!

Dave: but at the same time of course they'll tell you that this place is just a museum piece the future is flat floor bingo halls modern air conditioned buildings that's the future

Anna: and they're not going to invest

Dave: well they have they've got invest in this place

Anna: or maintain?

Dave: they've got to

Anna: don't they have to by law coz of english heritage?

Dave: oh yes yes they have to I mean they spent two million pounds four years ago but most of that was cosmetic in the sense it was new carpets new seats and a paint job

Anna: not structural

Dave: well it doesn't need anything structural to be honest it's a very solidly built building there's nothing structurally unsound about it at all the only sad part is the fact that the ceiling is now looking very grubby
pages.caption: Dave and Anna

pages.html:
Anna: very smoky in here isn't it and you can't stop people I suppose

Dave: but we could not afford to paint that because we would have to shut down and if we shut down the business would go you'd kiss it goodbye they'd go somewhere else they'd disappear and they wouldn't come back because of the time... it would take several weeks to paint that, to scaffold it out and paint it they'd get comfortable somewhere else and you'd never get them back. so the best protection for this building is for it to make money

Anna: so they're not very loyal bingo people

Dave: they're not I'm afraid they'll go where ever they think they can get the best deal...

-end-
pages.caption: Dave and Anna
